newsitem.title: USA: Clinton in the South, Dole criss-crosses U.S..
newsitem.headline: Clinton in the South, Dole criss-crosses U.S..

text.p: President Bill Clinton tried to keep campaign finance questions from slowing his momentum on Saturday while a sleepless Bob Dole launched the second day of his round-the-clock push for the White House.

On a southern swing in the final days before Tuesday's election, Democrat Clinton opened the day in Texas, one of the few big U.S. states where polls say he is trailing his Republican opponent. He had a morning rally scheduled at the Alamo in San Antonio with his wife Hillary.
But before the president's first appearance, Dole had already completed two campaign stops on the second day of a 96-hour cross-country race to what he hopes is a come-from-behind victory on Tuesday.

Before dawn, Dole was chatting up bleary-eyed Americans in a New Jersey coffee shop. Then he flew to breakfast in a Philadelphia suburb where he appeared with former Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Colin Powell. The candidate said he had gotten about an hour of sleep over a 24-hour period.

Clinton was trying to keep an election finance affair from eroding the lead he has held for months in public opinion polls. With public attention focused on campaign contributions to the Democrats from wealthy foreigners, some polls showed the race narrowing.

A Reuters tracking poll suggested on Friday the campaign finance issue was hurting Clinton, clipping his lead to just 5.5 percentage points over Dole -- 42 percent to 36.5 percent. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot had 8.4 percent. The poll's margin of error was three points.
Friday's CNN/USAToday/Gallup poll showed Clinton leading by a much bigger margin, 18 points, but it also showed Perot enjoying a late surge to 10 percent.

Indeed Perot, a wealthy Texan who has long presented himself as the alternative to politics-as-usual in Washington, appeared energised by the campaign finance issue and continued hammering away at the issue on Friday in hopes of drawing even more voters to his column.

Perot poured scorn on the fact that Clinton had delivered a speech calling for an overhaul of campaign finance laws. "He (Clinton) won't talk to you at all about whether he did it or not but he comes out and says let's fix it," Perot said.

Clinton on Friday insisted he and his party had "played by the rules" in collecting campaign money. But he called for changes in the laws that he said in the past were blocked by Dole, a 35-year veteran of Congress.

Top officials of the Democratic National Committee acknowledged in interviews published on Saturday in The Washington Post and The New York Times that under pressure to keep up with Republican fund-raising efforts they had not adequately scrutinised donors.

Clinton later on Saturday was to make an airport stop in his hometown of Little Rock, Arkansas, and a final pre-election visit to Florida, where he is leading in the polls but by a relatively small margin.
The biggest worry for the Clinton camp appeared to be voter turnout, which would be important in what the White House hopes will be a victory of more than 50 percent of the final vote.
Clinton won the White House with just 43 percent of the vote in 1992, in a three-way race with Perot and President George Bush.
One sign of Clinton's relative confidence was his decision to cancel an election-eve visit to California.

Meanwhile, by the end of Saturday alone, Dole planned to visit at least eight states. On Saturday morning in Essington, Pennsylvania, Powell told several hundred people crowded into a restaurant that Dole could still emerge victorious.
"It's winnable and he's going to win it," Powell declared.
